frames.narration: A team must export a report as CSV. One function does it. Someone says: JSON, XML and PDF are coming, so build for them now.

The speculative version adds an exporter registry, a config file and a factory, plus two exporters for formats nobody asked for. It costs 9 touch points to build, against 3 for the plain function, and 6 options now sit unused.
One report now goes through 7 calls instead of 1. Nothing is wrong, so nobody removes it, and every reader of this code has to trace through it.

Over the year, 10 internal change requests arrive. Plain code takes each in 2 touch points. The layers take a guessed change in 1, but a change that does not fit the interface in 4. At a 50% hit rate the layers cost 25 for the ten changes, plain code 20.

Now the other kind of decision. The team also shipped a stored file format with no version field. Old readers sit in other teams' programs and in files on disk, and you cannot update them in one commit.

A new currency field is added. An old reader does not error: it reads the currency as part of the name and carries on with wrong data. Adding the field late costs 9 touch points per change on a public API and 15 on a stored format, in this model.
Planning ahead here costs 2 points: a version field, and a rule that a reader rejects versions it does not know. The new record is now refused loudly by old readers, and read correctly by new ones.
The rule: keep internal code plain and add structure when a real request shows its shape. Spend the foresight on what is costly to reverse, such as the contract that other people's code depends on.
